en: On the Beginning and End of Composing this Commentary:
Alas! To propagate the sutras is difficult; to propagate the Lotus Sutra is even more difficult. To propagate the Lotus Sutra through mere oral exposition is already difficult;
to compose a commentary upon it is even more so. I have experienced this myself and thus believe it deeply. My clan’s origins...
He was a native of Xin-yi in Ji Prefecture. His family name was Zhao, and his parents were of humble means; unable to provide for him, he left home at the age of eight to enter the monastic life.
He initially served as an attendant to a local farmer, who was likewise unable to instruct him. He therefore went to study under his grandfather, where he first engaged in the Confucian classics.

After two years, he had a fair understanding of the meanings of the characters and occasionally practiced recitation, devoting himself solely to his daily lessons. This was when he was eleven years old.
I followed my Master to the home of the donor, Lord Yuan. While the assembly of monks was reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Lord jokingly said to me, "This śrāmaṇera has received my offerings;
can he recite the sūtra for me? I replied, "Yes. Thereupon, I joined the assembly in recitation as if it were the result of lifelong practice.
The entire congregation was amazed, and my Master was also filled with joy. He then stroked my head and, before the assembly, declared: "This..."
"You must have come from among the monastic community. He followed [Master] Xiuyun for his full ordination according to seniority and studied the Vinaya scriptures with some diligence;

he was filled with enthusiasm, constantly keeping in mind the study of the teachings. Initially, he listened to the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing* (Lotus Sūtra) under Master Shanying, and subsequently, he listened to the *Shoulengyan Jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra) under Master Yanfa.
He was entirely at a loss and understood nothing. Later, in the second year of the Yongzheng era (Jiachen), he visited Mount Yan to pay his respects and listen to the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Whenever he encountered difficult passages, he would suddenly attain new insights that differed from previous explanations. When he presented these to Master Gong, Gong gave him his profound approval.
Thereupon, he conceived the intention to comment upon the scripture. After one year had passed, he retired to live among the rocks and grasses of Mount Miaofeng.

In the vihāra, he took up his brush to begin his commentary. Upon reaching the opening passage of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*), which offers a double eulogy of wisdom, a sense of doubt suddenly arose within him.
For fifteen days he was unable to compose a single word.

He read through the text by day and contemplated it until the third watch of the night, until eventually his sight and hearing became dim and he lost all appetite for food. At that time, Guangxiu was by his side and laughed at him, thinking:
He had entered the realm of Māra. One day, while reading the sutra, he reached the passage "Thus have I heard. Suddenly, he attained a realization.
For the first time, he believed that what the ancients said—that "mountains, rivers, and the great earth are entirely the manifestation of the Dharma King’s body"—was not a deception.
From then on, not only did he become free from doubt regarding this sutra, but even when he examined all the various scriptures, they were likewise entirely clear to him.
I was hesitant. When I intended to continue the composition, disputes arose in secret; the roles of host and guest were ill-suited, and my original aspiration remained unfulfilled.

Subsequently, Xiu-yun arrived, followed by Sheng-gan. Before their feet had even crossed the threshold, suspicion and jealousy arose. Fortunately, I recognized these as obstacles to the Dharma, and my resolve did not waver.
Xiu-yun continued the previous draft, while Sheng-gan recorded the topical outlines (*kepan*); however, they ultimately could not overcome [the difficulties].

I resigned and withdrew to Xichan Temple, supporting myself by begging for food. Intending to fulfill my original resolve, before long adverse conditions were exhausted, yet favorable obstacles soon arose.
Summoned by the Office of the Sangha Registrar, I was appointed as an instructor at Wanshan Hall.

Having resided there for two years, I have been occupied with the monastic curriculum and ritual protocols; having no leisure for these duties, what mind could I have set upon literary composition? (Gengxu year)
In winter, I took my leave of Wanshan and resided at Yiguang. There, the walls could not shield my body from the elements, and the room could hardly block out the sun.

As the days raced across the earth and wood, time was constantly consumed by my hurried activities. Although I occasionally held lectures and established schedules, these were merely undertaken to fulfill the expectations of those who came to study;

I had no leisure to thoroughly complete this commentary. In the spring of the Gui-chou year, I resolved to close myself within a retreat and once again attend to my previous draft. Hardly had I begun...
He completed the *Zhengzong* (Correct Lineage).

Furthermore, he encountered an imperial decree ordering him to the Yuanming Garden to collate texts such as the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) by imperial command. Consequently, he devoted his daily efforts to the brush and ink, synthesizing the views of past and present.

I believe my humble observations may offer some slight benefit. At that time, I reflected that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the king of all scriptures, and Qingliang [Zongmi] holds the preeminent position within this tradition.
Without investigating its source, how can one encompass its branches? It was for this reason that, in the sixth year of the Qianlong era, the Xin-you year, I began this work.

I inaugurated the Huayan lecture period and devoted my heart to the Great Commentary (*Da shu*). Through three cycles of summer and winter, I gazed upon the vast depth of the great ocean while disparaging my own puddles;
I beheld the expansive breadth of the great void while feeling ashamed to boast of a mustard seed filling space.

In the winter of the Jiǎzǐ year, I lectured on this scripture once more and re-edited this commentary; before my work was half-finished, I had to depart for another invitation. In the winter of the Yǐchū year, I returned from Mount Qingliang.

I vow to fulfill this resolve. I shall seal the gates of uncertainty until the appointed time and await the day of completion. With my heart, I pray to the Triple Gem, relying on their compassion to sustain my spirit;
with my body, I exert myself through the six periods of the day, continuing from dawn to dusk as I attend to my studies. Thus, I record the conclusion of this work.
It was during the spring of the Bingyin year, in the month of Jichen. Yet, ever since I recall the age when I drove away crows, I have recited this naturally without formal study.

At the time I carried my book-box [to school], upon hearing it but once, its subtle meaning became clear; it seemed there was a karmic affinity from a previous life, and thus I ventured to compose it. Consequently, more than twenty years have passed;

though the draft has been revised three times and the text is roughly settled, the carving for publication has not yet occurred. Furthermore, during this interval— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "且其間順" (qiě qí jiān shùn), which translates as "Furthermore, during this interval..."*

They attacked one another in turn; it was severed and then resumed again and again. Had it not been for the Tathāgata’s distant vision and protection, his resolve would have been nearly ruined by adverse circumstances.
How grave indeed is the difficulty—and even greater the difficulty—of composing these commentaries! Nevertheless, over more than twenty years, I have regarded this as if it were but a dream-period.
Whether dwelling here or there, looking back, I am like a person within a dream. Nearly four hundred thousand [words] have passed.
I say: all these words are but the mutterings of sleep within a dream. Whether they accord with or oppose reality, they are all but the realms experienced within a dream.

Thus, as I now compile and arrange this from beginning to end, it remains nothing more than dreaming within a dream. I humbly entreat those who read my commentary hereafter and dwell within its sphere of experience [to understand this].
All should contemplate in this manner.
Recorded respectfully by the junior disciple Tongli of the Xianzong school on the Buddha’s Birthday in the month of Zhonglü,

Regarding the preface to this separate edition:

since this sutra has circulated in China, commentaries, sub-commentaries, and treatises have become exceedingly numerous. Their texts are rich and their meanings are vast; indeed, they surpass the original *Wenju*.

Yet, in gathering the gold and collecting the jade, none have achieved such great perfection as this. Now, for the sake of guiding beginners and leading them gradually into the inner sanctum, I have compiled this work.
There are differing interpretations from previous commentaries; fearing that new views might cause alarm, you should strive to examine them thoroughly and not hastily dismiss them with doubt.
This commentary is titled *Zhǐzhǎng* (Pointing at the Palm), intended to be clear and easy to understand. I have not avoided providing philological explanations, though some may involve prolixity.

Since intellectual fruition transcends conventional boundaries, one may freely abandon the complex for the essential. My own position is like leaning against a wall for support; for now, one must proceed by way of the coarse.
I am a person of humble station; do not disdain my picking at leaves and tracing branches. Do not let me omit ten while hanging on to one. (Regarding the underlying principle:
Having lost the opportunity for formal study in my youth, my wisdom does not surpass that of others. I have not yet been able to visit every eminent scholar nor extensively peruse ancient writings.
Much of what flows from my breast in these commentaries consists of single words and phrases; as I am not skilled in the compositions of others, I dare not [claim otherwise].
They enter [the Way] spontaneously; there is no deliberate rejection or exclusion. Do not insist on right or wrong.
A single sound reaches all perfectly, yet diverse interpretations each manifest. As with the pestle, mortar, rope, and winnowing basket, they all describe the likeness of the elephant’s body;
as for the crane, snow, conch, and rice, which can clarify the true color of the milk? Seeking the root through the branches, each selects its own rationale. Thus one enters the Path.
Circumstances have been manifold and sufficient; do not say that such abundance of matters hinders its wide dissemination.
Both the Tiantai and Xian (Huayan) schools, in verifying the sequence of the Dharma, frequently cite parables from the *Lotus Sūtra*.

For instance, they cite the parable of the burning house to describe matters of fear, using them to verify that the Great Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* is difficult for beings to receive. This has been universally followed by both ancient and modern masters, and it seems there is no [contradiction].
This may be discussed. Now, to simplify [the Four Noble Truths] by rendering them as merely the "Truth of Suffering" is far too abrupt and superficial.

One should know that those who cite scriptural evidence do so to capture the general outline (*mahā-uddāna*), sometimes neglecting the specific details (*aṅga*). Those who compose commentaries distinguish these specific details;

they do not merely pretend to match the general outline, for they clearly know they would otherwise contradict the ancients. Yet, fearing to go against the scriptures, I have presented this. May the noble and wise examine it and graciously grant their forgiveness. All.
Such instances need not be recounted exhaustively.
Within the structural framework of a single scripture, there are both main threads and sub-items; within these sub-items, there are further threads and items.

This is like the succession of generations—grandfather, son, grandson, and father—arising one after another without the slightest confusion. As for the relationship between main threads and main threads, or sub-items and sub-items, it is as follows:
Just as brothers follow one another in succession, where priority and sequence are appropriate, so too does this division of sections possess its own natural order.
The *Lengyan zhengmo* (The True Pulse of the Śūraṅgama) has largely captured this secret; I have now modeled my commentary upon it.

However, Master Jiao’s analysis was overly exhaustive, frequently interrupting what should have been continuous and thus causing the meaning to lack coherence for beginners who fail to perceive this. In my current commentary, I have distinguished these points.
In order to avoid excessive fragmentation in this continuation, there are instances where a single section contains two or three distinct meanings.

If these were not clearly delineated, it would be impossible to distinguish their differences or similarities; therefore, I have used circles (○) in the main text to mark them. In the commentary (*śāstra*), each meaning is individually identified:
for instance, at the beginning, it says "First, [meaning X]," and upon completion of that explanation, the next is marked as "[Meaning Y]."
I set forth my intention here, hoping that it will not be overly prolix while still ensuring that the essential points are clearly distinguished.
In ancient commentaries, the topical outlines (*mukō*) often do not include all sub-sections; for instance, if a section is divided into three parts, only the first is typically indicated.
Furthermore, [the text] was divided into sections or inserted into the prose, which made it particularly difficult for beginners to cross-reference and verify.

Now, following the structural outline (*ke-shiki*) of the *Mida Shōsho*, I have marked all divisions and subsequently correlated them with the main text. Once the commentary is finished, I shall conclude each section by stating "The [Name] Section is Complete.
However, if two sections are very closely adjacent, I will not repeat this conclusion to facilitate reading and avoid excessive complexity.

Turning the front upward and the back downward, the *Lengyan zhengmai* (The True Pulse of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) employs characters such as "A," "B," and so forth to distinguish the categories and their hierarchical order;

the Elder Boting also frequently adopted this practice. In this present commentary, the categories are fully indicated throughout, and at the conclusion of each section, they are again summarized from beginning to end.
The sequence is clearly evident; therefore, I have not further added characters such as "A" or "B.

In the parables within the sutras, the ancient commentaries all establish topical divisions based on the metaphors themselves—such as, for instance, the metaphors of abandoning the small table and using the chariot found in the "Parable of the Burning House.
Regarding the actual teachings (*dharma*), they merely add the character "correspondence" (*he*) and do not explicitly reveal the teaching itself, which results in the meaning of the teaching...

The meaning is hidden within the metaphors; it is only through thorough investigation that it becomes clear. In this commentary, the section on metaphors is established strictly according to the Dharma.

For instance, the metaphor of "discarding the stool and using the cart" is easily understood as a metaphor for abandoning the provisional and employing the real, and so forth. Within these [explanations of] the Dharma, one simply removes the word "metaphor."
It is hoped that the meaning of the Dharma will be made manifest within these analogies so that it may be seen immediately without the need for exhaustive study.
Regarding the topical outlines of these verses, the ancient commentaries all categorized them by the number of lines; however, this makes them particularly difficult to remember during oral lectures.
Upon careful examination, this method is not particularly essential.

Since the phrase "original text" (běnwén) has already been appended beneath each section, the preceding and following divisions are sufficient to distinguish them; therefore, the number of lines is not recorded here.

In ancient commentaries, the titles of the chapters were placed outside the topical divisions (*ke*), while the verses were mixed within them; thus, one appeared to have no fixed location, and the other seemed to be confused with the gāthās.
In this present commentary, each is settled according to its proper section. When encountering a chapter title, it is stated:

"At this point there is a chapter title," or the title is directly indicated as "So-and-so. Once the explanation is concluded, it is then stated: "The sutra text is divided into [such-and-such] sections. When encountering...
Regarding the headings (biaoshou): one should state, "There is a heading here," or simply say, "The heading is such-and-such.

Once the commentary is finished, one should then state how many sections the main verse (zhengsong) consists of. The lecturer should follow this method so that the titles have a clear point of reference and the headings do not become confused.
When Master Kumārajīva divided the sūtra, the text consisted of seven fascicles. When the commentary (*śāstra*) was appended, the seven fascicles could no longer contain it all.

Some ancient masters separately divided the volume headings, which inevitably deviated from the original intent of the translator. Now, the volume headings of the commentary shall remain as they were;
however, where the text is excessively voluminous, it shall be divided, with the title marked as "Part [X] of Fascicle [Y]" or "Fascicle [Y]."
This is done out of deep reverence for the Buddha-dharma and a lack of audacity to alter it arbitrarily.
Where the commentaries composed by ancient masters occasionally accord with my own views, I have also made slight selections from them.
If I were to use their words in their entirety, I would cite their names, such as saying "Dacheng says," and so forth. If there is even a slight modification, [I do not attribute it to them].
Thus, when I speak of the "Great Accomplishment" (*Mahāsiddhi*) and so forth, it is because I dare not conceal the excellence of the ancients.
The ten gates preceding this sutra have already been roughly established; the phrasing generally follows brevity, and the meaning especially avoids prolixity.

This is because I consider a little to be sufficient, seeking only that others may easily uphold [the teaching] rather than forcing them to conform to me, and disregarding the potential for the sutra to be compromised. Later, while lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*...
Having read the Great Commentary, I realized that nothing but the elaborate could exhaustively convey the subtle marvels, while nothing but the concise could capture the artisan’s genius.

Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Avataṃsaka* serve as the beginning and the end of one another; if one does not model oneself after their profound discourses, there is a fear of remaining ignorant of this perfect principle.

Therefore, I have re-composed this work, which differs from what was previously heard. Compared to the ordinary, it seems extensive; compared to those [great scriptures], it is still brief. One should understand this well.
This is appropriate.

This "Exposé of the Perfect Fusion" outlines the essential principles of the Dharma: it is profound stillness and empty vacuity; neither provisional nor real; both three and one; and it blends the myriad transformations into a single unity.
A single entity, standing apart from all phenomena and existing alone, which cannot be grasped by thought—can this be anything other than the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?
When the provisional is unified with the real, and the three are discarded to establish the one; even if one were to point to the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), they would exhaust all contemplation.
Sharing its brilliance with the *Avataṃsaka*, it eclipses all other sights with its solitary radiance. Can this, too, be anything other than the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*)?
Is it not the Lotus Sūtra? Therefore, our World-Honored One, having realized this Dharma-seal, manifested at the site of enlightenment;

he suspended the wheel of wisdom upon the high mountain and proclaimed the profound mystery throughout the Dharma-realm. Out of compassion for the impoverished sons, he temporarily laid aside his precious robes and divided the teachings to accord with the capacities of the times.

Thus, the three vehicles were gradually opened across the various assemblies. Now, intending to withdraw his radiance into the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), he nevertheless considers returning to illuminate all beings once more.
Xiongfeng specifically traveled to Mount Ling to assemble a vast congregation of those with karmic affinity, serving as a preliminary guide.
He expounded the subtle words of the *Unlimited Meanings* to fully reveal the later school’s tenet, and extended a single hair’s light to shine afar.

As Maitreya poses his inquiry today, Mañjuśrī provides the verified response based on past causes. Since the true mechanism has been disclosed, how could one remain silent? Thus, as soon as the samādhi first arose—

The two wisdoms were repeatedly extolled, while a multitude of doubts assailed the minds of the assembly. While the three requests were uniquely earnest from the part of Śāriputra, [the Buddha] sought to strengthen the hearts of the multitude;
he excluded the five thousand from the teaching to eliminate their arrogance, thereby inspiring true faith. This was as rare as the appearance of a single udumbara flower.
Whether describing himself or others, his intent in manifesting in the world was entirely the same; whether speaking of the provisional or the real, he revealed the entry [into truth].
The great system of literary and institutional norms is now fixed. Those of superior capacity have already attained awakening, yet those of middling capacity still remain deluded.

He records the signs of the transmission to Huaguang and provides metaphors to answer the request of Śāriputra. This may be compared to an elder whose house has caught fire while his foolish son is playing within it.
Unaware and unconscious, the compassionate father heard of this from outside; unable to save them, he could not find peace. He permitted three carriages and gave one vehicle.
Knowing the elder’s intention was born of true sincerity, [the disciples] opened up the Three Vehicles to reveal the Single Path.

Believing that the Tathāgata’s words are without falsehood, the followers of the Two Vehicles recounted their persistent delusions and compared themselves to impoverished sons. The four sons alike presented their faith and understanding.

It is fitting to entrust this family treasure. [The Buddha] advanced the teaching that rain has no dual moisture; while the differences lie in the objects [receiving it], he caused them to know that the Dharma is fundamentally of one flavor.

That its depth or shallowness arises from the capacity of the recipient, he then universally bestowed as the prediction of fruition. Having fully demonstrated these parables and explanations, he further separately opened up the causes and conditions.
He draws in those of inferior faculties so they do not fall, and together they travel to the treasure-place, where all are equally recorded for the Buddha-vehicle.

The bright pearl within the robe points to a close friend; having already studied and revolved [in the cycle], one admires his fragrant traces, while the Tathāgata bestows true compassion upon them as well.
Desiring to manifest the merit of universal salvation, he uses the Medicine King to reveal this benefit; to clarify the power of his great vow, he thus borrows from many...

Treasure this and pray for its realization. Abandon the reckless wisdom of mere intellectual speculation and apply yourself to cultivation. Contemplate how the Buddha Kāśyapa planted the seeds of his cause over many kalpas;

from this, one should know the value of shame and remorse. Seeing that those of dull faculties pushed back the holy realm as something unattainable, yet observing that the Dragon Girl attained the fruit of enlightenment in a single moment, one should likewise exert one's strength.

Thus, I have taken up this burden upon one shoulder, fortunate that the paradigm of this Way has found its rightful successor. I hold fast to the four practices, rejoicing that the handle for warding off difficulties possesses the proper method.
Furthermore, I consider that those newly recorded as Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas at the initial stage possess but shallow and narrow intellectual capacity.

Unable to provide broad salvation, he therefore relied upon bodhisattvas from other regions to request the mandate to propagate the sutras and summoned his own disciples from their original lands to grandly inherit the Buddha-way.
Bodhisattvas who were to succeed him became confused by immediate traces and lost sight of the distant cause; thus, the Father was described as young while the Son was old.
The Tamer of Men from Central India, relying on his original lifespan to manifest wondrous efficacy, cited the analogy of the skilled physician who turned his back on his son.

The great merit having been manifested, the gates of delusion and attachment were thereby opened. Not only did those of new renown and Śrāvakas, as well as Bodhisattvas at the initial stage, suddenly perceive their bodies ascending to the Wondrous Peak;
from this point on, those of profound rank and superior status, these lofty sages who have accumulated meritorious conduct, proceed as if traveling by spirit to the Fragrant Sea.
Discerning his merits, one finds that these merits are immeasurable; when weighing the causes of his blessings, those causes of fortune have no boundaries.

That his six sense-faculties were purified is clearly evidenced by the testimony of the *Adhimātra-pūjaka* (Never-Despising One); that he was reviled by the fourfold assembly and received the retribution of Avīci Hell is not false.
The Bodhisattvas who sprang from the earth made great vows in the lands of his emanations; after his passing, they propagated the sutra, serving merely as—
I perceive the profound grace bestowed upon me by this Lion among Men, who manifests supernatural powers within this boundless ocean-like assembly.

While receiving his timely praise, he spoke with a firm and unyielding resolve; as he was about to descend from the Dharma seat, he exhorted me most earnestly, fearing I might fall into a deviant path, and once again provided a model for my conduct.
Indeed, I have been able to exhaust my attachment to self and dharmas, just as King Bhaiṣajyarāja burned his own body, purifying both the defiled and the pure.

When attachments are forgotten, it is like the arrival of wondrous sounds from afar; one must then respond without fixed form or circumference, re-entering the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) to assist in cultivating the provisional yet secret merit, guarding the mind through the power of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When these four dharmas are accomplished, one should practice with diligent cultivation for twenty-one days.

That this sutra will certainly be attained is beyond doubt. Because Samantabhadra manifests his body through his vows, it shall circulate in this manner, and its circulation shall be without obstruction.
Thus, how could it be that this sutra alone follows such a sequence? It is simply that when the Holy Brush shone eastward, the entire transformation was fully revealed;
when the Assembly of Worthies came from the West, the four dharmas were shown once more. From the very beginning, it was indeed thus.
Having subsumed the latter, how could one ever have omitted the former? Furthermore, the nature of words and letters is empty; emptiness admits nothing that it does not encompass.
The essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is all-pervasive; its pervasiveness leaves nothing unprovided for. Thus, a single word or a single phrase can penetrate infinite and boundless meanings.
Whether receiving or upholding them, they become the most perfect and wondrous cause. Since the principle is fully contained within phenomena, it accords with each phenomenon, one by one.
Both are manifested; these are also the phenomena of the complete principle (*dharmatā*). Following this principle, each and every thing interpenetrates one another.

Thus, the three transformations of the lands are neither defiled nor pure; the divided bodies all arrive, being neither one nor many. Many kalpas and half a day are simultaneous in their extension and contraction;
birth-and-death and eternal abiding coexist in both concealment and manifestation. The marks of the tongue and the radiance of the body hairs reach from Vulture Peak upward to the heavens.
From the Brahma world, a snap of the fingers or a cough resounds far and wide throughout the ten directions from this Sahā world.
All these things transcend the traces of the mind and cut off the path of words; they were not seen at other times, yet they are not unheard by those with the proper capacity.

I long for the wondrous Truth, yearning to return while adrift in exile; I am lost on the path and find it difficult to go home. Fortunately, through a slight affinity, I have been able to behold the sacred scriptures.

Regarding them as my own parents, I shall uphold and propagate them for the rest of my life. Yet, in seeking the essential meaning within vast learning, I have appended flowery words to the profound principles.
I am well aware that the Buddha-way is like a mountain—ant-like steps can never reach its summit—and that the sagely wisdom is like the ocean.
How could the measure of a ladle suffice to compare with its source? For now, relying on my own humble views, I shall briefly guide the ignorant youth;

thus, I have selected what is clear and easy to understand, titling this work "Pointing to the Palm. Furthermore, I prostrate myself with all five limbs and take refuge in the Triple Gem, extending this sincere devotion to pray for your compassionate protection.
I prostrate to the Lord of Dharma preaching on Vulture Peak, To the Honored One Prabhūtaratna who realized the sutra through his vows,
To the infinite Buddhas of the manifested bodies gathered like clouds, To the wondrous Lotus Flower of the True Mark of the One Vehicle,
And to the two assemblies of monks— those long resident and those newly emerged. May the inexhaustible Triple Gem grant me their protection and guidance.
May that which I have undertaken be swiftly and perfectly accomplished, so that its circulation and benefit may be inexhaustible.
